title: Deep sleep's embrace
hookLine: the best night's sleep you ever had, with nothing in it, and something that still woke up rested
carry: in deep sleep, the self is still there
tomorrow: death — the caterpillar reaching the next blade
last: THE SELF LIGHTS EVEN YOUR DREAMS.

cards: Some nights you sleep so deeply there's nothing to report. No dream, no time passing, no you. Then the alarm, and you sit up and say, I slept like a stone.
It's the best sleep there is, and nobody was there to enjoy it. Or was there? Who, exactly, slept well?
Yajnavalkya takes King Janaka one floor below the dreams, to the place you go every night and never remember.

teach.b: As a falcon or an eagle, Yajnavalkya says, tired from circling all day in the sky, folds its wings and heads home to its nest, so a person hurries to that state where, asleep, he wants nothing and sees no dream.
Then the image this day is named for.

teach.h: HELD, KNOWING NOTHING OUTSIDE OR IN.
teach.b: As a man held by the one he loves knows nothing outside and nothing inside, so a person held by the knowing self knows nothing outside and nothing inside.
That is the form, the text says, where every desire is met, so there's no desire at all, and no sorrow. Then a startling list.

teach.h: A FATHER IS NOT A FATHER.
teach.b: There, a father is not a father, a mother not a mother. Gods are not gods. A thief is not a thief.
Untouched by good, untouched by evil, he has crossed every sorrow of the heart. Nothing you are in daylight follows you in. And yet the text insists this isn't a blank.
When he doesn't see there, he is still seeing, for the seer's seeing is never lost. There's just no second thing to see. Vedanta teachers draw a well-known clue from this.
You wake up and say, I slept well; I knew nothing. Who knew it was good?

teach.h: IN DEEP SLEEP, THE SELF IS STILL THERE.
teach.b: Someone was there: the self, resting with no roles at all. Not a daughter, not a student, not a worrier. That's the teaching: you are not your roles; the self is there even when every role is gone.

In the Chandogya, Indra feared deep sleep was like being destroyed; here Yajnavalkya calls it an embrace. The Mandukya, which you met last year, names this state prajna, the third of the self's four quarters.

how: Vedanta teachers use deep sleep, described here and in the Mandukya Upanishad, as an everyday clue to the self: something rests, and on waking, one knows one slept well.

o: the dream state, where the sleeper builds a world
no dream, no desire: held, with nothing outside or in
a sleep like death, where the self is destroyed

games.q: what's inside the passage — tap the pairs.
p: folds its wings and goes home
the knowing self; the third state

s: the text says deep sleep is a blank where nothing is seen
the seer's seeing is never lost; there's just no second thing to see.
Indra in the Chandogya and Yajnavalkya here view deep sleep differently
Indra worried it was like being destroyed; Yajnavalkya calls it an embrace.
Vedanta teachers point to waking up and saying 'I slept well' as a clue the self was there
someone knew the sleep was good, though nothing was seen.

games.q: you're a falcon that's been circling all day. you're tired. what do you do?
o: keep circling; there's more to see.
fold your wings and head for the nest.
games.why: it folds its wings and heads home. so a person hurries to that state where, asleep, he wants nothing and sees no dream.

practice: Picture the falcon, tired, circling lower and lower, and with each out-breath fold something in: your plans for tonight, your name, your job, the role you play for other people.
You're not trying to fall asleep, only letting the day's sky go, and resting in the nest with nothing outside to watch and nothing inside to fix.

wordCard.voice: Deep sleep. No dream, no desire, no sorrow: a person held by prajna, the knowing self, with nothing outside and nothing inside. In the Mandukya, the third state.

orig.note: Sanskrit prājña: the knowing one, from pra + jñā, to know. the self in deep sleep (4.3.21; Mandukya 5).

carryVoice: Your line: in deep sleep, the self is still there. The seer's seeing is never lost. Sleep well.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.11.1–2 (Indra's doubt about deep sleep)
